title: Nuclear Energy
scope: Fission reactors for electricity. Civilian power, not weapons.

overview.summary: Nuclear supplies about a tenth of world electricity; nations are split on building more, extending old plants, or shifting fully to renewables.
overview.scope_covered: Civilian fission power: costs, safety, waste disposal, new construction, plant life extension, and small modular reactors.
overview.scope_excluded: Nuclear weapons, fusion research, and non-electric uses such as naval propulsion or medical isotope production.
overview.why_now: In August 2026 the IEA published a major report on nuclear power’s role in secure, net-zero energy transitions, and the 2025 World Nuclear Industry Status Report tracked newbuild, SMR and decommissioning trends across the global fleet.

stats.label: Nuclear share of global electricity
stats.note: Nuclear plants supplied about 9 percent of the world’s electricity in 2023, making nuclear the second largest source of low-carbon power after hydroelectric dams.
stats.detail: The figure comes from total nuclear generation of 2,602 terawatt-hours in 2023 divided by global electricity output. It counts only electricity, not total energy use: the fuels burned for transport, industrial heat and home heating sit outside the denominator, so nuclear’s share of all the energy people consume is smaller still. The share has also come down over time. Nuclear supplied 16.5 percent of the world’s electricity in 1997, and the standard reference account attributes the fall since then in large part to the economics of nuclear power becoming more difficult rather than to any collapse in output.

stats.label: Civilian reactors operating worldwide
stats.note: Nuclear power plants supplied 2,602 terawatt hours of electricity in 2023, about 9 percent of global electricity generation, making nuclear the second largest low-carbon source after hydroelectricity.
stats.detail: The count covers civilian fission reactors that generate electricity for public grids, not naval propulsion units or the small research and isotope reactors run by universities and laboratories. It counts reactors, not stations, so a plant with several units adds several to the total. As of November 2025 those 416 reactors carried an overall capacity of 376 GW, and the average global capacity factor is 89%, about nine-tenths of what continuous full power would yield. Listing is a matter of licensed status rather than daily output, so reactors idled for maintenance or awaiting clearance to restart remain inside the number.

stats.label: Levelized cost: nuclear, onshore wind, solar
stats.note: New nuclear plants are estimated to produce electricity at 69 dollars per megawatt-hour, more expensive than onshore wind or utility-scale solar, but the cheapest option among dispatchable, always-available power sources.
stats.detail: These are median levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) estimates from a joint analysis by the International Energy Agency and the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency, for an nth-of-a-kind plant completed in 2025 at a 7 percent discount rate. LCOE does not fully capture the value of dispatchability: wind and solar are cheaper per unit of energy but are intermittent, so a direct comparison understates what nuclear (and other always-on sources) contribute to grid reliability. Among strictly dispatchable technologies, the same analysis found nuclear to be the least-cost option, cheaper than coal at 88 dollars/MWh or gas at 71 dollars/MWh once a 30 dollar per ton carbon price is applied.

stats.label: Cost of power from life-extended reactors
stats.note: Extending the operating life of an existing nuclear plant, rather than building a new one, produces the cheapest dispatchable electricity of any option examined, at 32 dollars per megawatt-hour.
stats.detail: This figure comes from the same IEA and NEA cost analysis that priced new nuclear at 69 dollars/MWh. Because an existing reactor’s large upfront capital cost has already been paid off, keeping it running simply requires maintenance, safety upgrades, and fuel, which is far cheaper than financing new construction. This is one reason many countries, including the United States, have prioritized license extensions for existing reactors over building new ones.

stats.label: Life-cycle CO2 per kWh: nuclear, gas, coal
stats.note: Counting emissions from construction, fuel mining, and plant operation, nuclear power’s embodied total life-cycle emission intensity has a median value of 12 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour, the lowest among all commercial baseload energy sources.
stats.detail: The figure comes from a 2014 Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change analysis of the carbon footprint literature, which reported a median embodied total life-cycle emission intensity for nuclear power of 12 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour. A life-cycle figure counts emissions embodied across a plant’s whole existence — mining and enriching the fuel, pouring the concrete, building and later dismantling the plant, and handling the waste — rather than only those released while it is generating electricity. That accounting matters for nuclear, whose reactors emit no greenhouse gases in operation but carry most of their footprint in construction and fuel supply. The same analysis puts coal at 820 and natural gas at 490 grams of CO2-equivalent per kilowatt-hour. As of 2021, one estimate credits nuclear reactors worldwide with having avoided 72 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions since 1970 compared with coal-fired generation.

stats.label: Deaths per terawatt-hour from nuclear
stats.note: Nuclear power’s historical death rate, counting both accidents and radiation exposure, is 0.03 deaths per terawatt-hour of electricity produced, making it the second-safest energy source after solar.
stats.detail: Deaths per terawatt-hour is a ratio rather than a total: the deaths attributed to an energy source divided by the electricity that source produced, which lets technologies of very different size be compared on the same footing. How such a figure is built depends on which deaths an analyst counts and over what span, so estimates for the same technology can differ. Coal, oil, natural gas, and hydropower have all caused more deaths per unit of energy generated, mainly through air pollution and industrial accidents rather than headline disasters. One estimate credits nuclear power with preventing about 1.84 million deaths from air pollution between 1971 and 2009 by displacing fossil-fuel generation that would otherwise have been burned.

stats.label: Fukushima radionuclide release vs Chernobyl
stats.note: UNSCEAR found that Fukushima released only about 10 percent of the radioiodine and radiocaesium that Chernobyl did, the two radionuclides considered most significant for radiation dose.
stats.detail: The number is a ratio of what escaped, not a measure of total harm. It compares the airborne release of the two isotopes that matter most for early health effects: radioiodine, which concentrates in the thyroid and drives dose in the first weeks, and radiocaesium, which governs longer-term ground contamination. Two things independent of the amount released shape what a given release means for people. One is where the plume travels, since material carried out over open ocean deposits far less on inhabited land than material carried across populated country. The other is how quickly authorities act, because most thyroid dose from an accident reaches people through contaminated milk, produce and drinking water, and prompt restrictions can cut that pathway off before it is walked. A release ratio holds none of this. It also leaves out the total radioactivity released in absolute terms, contamination of water and soil over time, the scale and duration of evacuation, and the economic and social costs that follow — dimensions on which the two accidents are compared by entirely different measures, and on which the ordering can differ from the one this figure suggests.
stats.source_label: UNSCEAR, “UNSCEAR 2020/2021 Fukushima Report – Frequently Asked Questions and Answers”

stats.label: Permanent high-level waste repositories operating
stats.note: No country in the world currently operates a commercial-scale, purpose-built underground repository for permanently disposing of high-level nuclear waste.
stats.detail: Spent nuclear fuel, the most radioactive category of nuclear waste, is instead held in interim storage, first in cooling pools for six to ten years and then in dry casks, at reactor sites or centralized facilities, pending a permanent solution. There is broad international consensus that deep geological repositories are the right long-term approach, and Finland’s Onkalo facility, serving the Olkiluoto plant, was under construction as of 2015 and is the furthest along toward becoming the first such repository. Until a repository opens, the absence of a permanent disposal path remains one of the most politically contentious aspects of nuclear power.

stats.label: Onkalo disposal depth below ground
stats.note: Finland’s Onkalo repository will place used nuclear fuel in bedrock about 430 meters underground, sealed inside iron-copper canisters.
stats.detail: The figure is a depth below the ground surface: it marks the level in the bedrock at which the disposal tunnels are excavated and the canisters of used fuel are emplaced. At that level each canister sits inside a multi-barrier system, in which every layer is meant to hold even if another fails: a tightly sealed iron-copper canister, a bentonite clay buffer packed around it, swelling clay backfill in the tunnels, engineered seals and plugs closing the tunnels and shafts, and the surrounding rock. The facility is designed to keep radioactive material isolated for at least 100,000 years and potentially up to a million years. Depth is one of the design parameters that serves that goal: it places the waste below the reach of surface erosion, weather, plant and animal life, and ordinary human activity, in rock where groundwater moves slowly and chemical conditions are stable enough to slow the corrosion of the canister.
stats.source_label: World Nuclear News, “Finnish regulator gives positive decision on used fuel repository”

stats.label: Vogtle 3 & 4 cost, first estimate to 2023
stats.note: The certified cost of building Vogtle’s two new reactors rose from 14 billion dollars at certification to about 34 billion dollars by 2023, with the main contractor Westinghouse going bankrupt partway through construction.
stats.detail: The 14 billion dollar figure was the certified construction and capital cost cited in the Seventeenth Semi-annual Vogtle Construction Monitoring Report of 2017, which blamed the contractor for not completing work as scheduled. Costs climbed further as delays continued: about 25 billion dollars by 2018, over 28.5 billion by 2021, and about 34 billion by 2023, with work still to be completed on Unit 4. Westinghouse Electric Company, the reactor supplier and lead contractor, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2017 because of losses on its two US nuclear construction projects (Vogtle and V.C. Summer), and in July 2017 Southern Nuclear took over construction from Westinghouse, choosing Bechtel that August as day-to-day construction manager for the rest of the project. The two units did eventually finish: Unit 3 entered commercial operation on July 31, 2023, and Unit 4 on April 29, 2024. The tile tracks the 2017-to-2023 progression of reported costs rather than any single final accounting, since published totals for the project vary with what is counted as construction, financing and ratepayer recovery.

stats.label: Hinkley Point C cost against approval estimate
stats.note: Hinkley Point C’s projected cost has climbed from an £18 billion approval estimate to £35 billion in 2015 prices, or about £48 billion in 2026 prices.
stats.detail: When the UK government and EDF approved Hinkley Point C in 2016, the project’s final cost was to be £18 billion in 2015 prices. As of 2026, the overall project cost is estimated at £35 billion in 2015 prices, or about £48 billion in 2026 prices, almost double the estimate when the project was approved. The two current figures describe the same station, one stated in the price levels of 2015 and one in those of 2026. Unit 1, the plant’s first reactor, is now projected to come online in 2030; when construction began in March 2017, completion was expected in 2025. The estimate rose in steps along the way: £19.6 billion, revised to £20.3 billion, in July 2017, £22–23 billion in January 2021, and £25–26 billion in May 2022, the later figures all in 2015 prices. The delays behind that growth include some caused by the COVID-19 pandemic and by Brexit, and they have produced significant budget overruns.
stats.source_label: Wikimedia Foundation, Inc., “Hinkley Point C nuclear power station”

stats.label: NuScale Idaho project cost before cancellation
stats.note: NuScale’s planned Idaho SMR plant saw its projected build cost roughly triple, from 3.6 billion to 9.3 billion dollars, before the project was scrapped in 2023.
stats.detail: The figures come from NuScale’s Carbon Free Power Project (CFPP) in Idaho, a plant that was to be built for Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems (UAMPS) at the Idaho National Laboratory. The projected build cost rose from 3.6 billion dollars for 720 MWe of capacity (as estimated in 2020) to 9.3 billion dollars for a smaller 462 MWe plant by January 2023. Facing this cost escalation and insufficient subscription from participating utilities, UAMPS and NuScale jointly canceled the project in November 2023, ending an agreement that had aimed to have reactors operating in Idaho by 2030. The range shown does not reflect a single consistent project scope, since the capacity being priced also shrank between the two estimates, so part of the per-unit cost increase reflects a smaller plant as well as broader cost growth.

stats.label: Rosatom share of new reactor orders, 2009-2018
stats.note: Rosatom, Russia’s state nuclear company, accounted for 23 of the 31 orders for new reactors placed worldwide between 2009 and 2018. On that count it is, as the tally’s source puts it, by far the largest player in international nuclear construction.
stats.detail: The figure comes from a tally of international nuclear construction orders placed over the decade 2009-2018: of 31 such orders, 23 went to Rosatom, putting its share at roughly three in four. An order here is a contract to build, so the measure tracks the export market for new reactor projects rather than anything about plants already running. Rosatom’s reach extends beyond simply building reactors; it also supplies reactor materials, enriches uranium, and handles waste disposal, functioning as a single supplier across the whole nuclear fuel chain. That vertical integration is what critics point to when arguing that Rosatom’s dominance gives Russia outsized leverage over countries, especially newcomers to nuclear power in the Middle East and Sub-Saharan Africa, that depend on it for a plant’s entire lifecycle rather than just its construction. A buyer choosing a Rosatom plant is choosing a decades-long relationship with one state-owned vendor, which is why the share of orders, and not only the eventual share of generating capacity, is treated as the telling number.

stats.label: UK nuclear capacity target for 2050
stats.note: The UK government aims for up to 24 gigawatts of nuclear power capacity by 2050, a target that could meet nearly a quarter of the country’s electricity demand.
stats.detail: This figure is a government ambition, not installed or contracted capacity: Great British Nuclear, the body set up to deliver the government’s long-term nuclear program, describes it as an ambition to deliver up to 24GW of nuclear power by 2050, which it says could meet nearly a quarter of the UK’s total power demand. GBN’s first priority is a competitive process to select small modular reactor technologies, which it says will underpin the government’s commitment to two nuclear project final investment decisions during the next Parliament, at least one of them an SMR project, with firms identified as best able to reach a decision by the end of 2029.

stats.label: Chinese reactor capital cost per kilowatt
stats.note: An independent analysis puts the average up-front capital cost of China’s 55 operating nuclear reactors at about 2,230 US dollars per kilowatt of gross capacity.
stats.detail: The figure comes from a GreenPrizm study of Chinese nuclear power plants, prepared for the Anthropocene Institute, that compiled construction budgets and financing data for reactors across China from public, mostly Chinese-language, sources. For the 55 reactors already in commercial operation as of year-end 2023, the study tallied total construction and financing costs of 841 billion yuan against 56.9 gigawatts of gross capacity, giving a unit cost of 14,755 yuan per kilowatt, converted at varying annual exchange rates to about 2,230 US dollars per kilowatt. Of that total, 79 percent was overnight construction cost and 21 percent was the cost of financing during construction. So the number is a fleet average of what it cost to build the plants, expressed per kilowatt of capacity, which is the standard way capital costs are compared across reactor designs and countries of very different sizes. It is a capital figure rather than a price of electricity: it says what was spent to put the capacity in place, not what the power sells for once the plant is running.
stats.source_label: GreenPrizm, 2023 Report on Chinese Nuclear Power Generation and Costs Analysis (Summary), prepared for the Anthropocene Institute

stats.label: Barakah contract cost, four units
stats.note: South Korea’s KEPCO-led consortium won a roughly 20.4 billion dollar contract to build, commission, and fuel all four Barakah reactors.
stats.detail: The 20.4 billion dollar figure is the value of the contract for construction, commissioning, and fuel loads for the four APR1400 units, and a high percentage of that contract was offered under a fixed-price arrangement. Separately, the consortium also expected to earn about another 20 billion dollars by jointly operating the reactors for 60 years, and Barakah One PJSC later took over management of about 24.4 billion dollars in project finances, comprising roughly 19.6 billion dollars in direct loans and 4.7 billion dollars in equity commitments from ENEC and KEPCO. So this figure is the initial build contract, not the full lifetime cost of the plant.
stats.source_label: world-nuclear.org, Nuclear Power in the United Arab Emirates

stats.label: Nuclear share of UAE electricity
stats.note: With all four Barakah units operating, nuclear power supplies about a quarter of the UAE’s electricity.
stats.detail: The plant generates roughly 40 terawatt-hours a year, which the source states equals about 25 percent of national electricity supply and avoids more than 22 million tonnes of carbon emissions annually. That share is measured against a grid that was almost entirely fossil-fueled beforehand: the source states that over 95 percent of UAE electricity came from fossil fuels prior to Barakah’s commissioning. For 2023 it reports total generation of 168 terawatt-hours, with nuclear supplying 33.1 terawatt-hours, or 20 percent.
stats.source_label: world-nuclear.org, Nuclear Power in the United Arab Emirates

stats.label: Kazakhstan share of EU uranium deliveries
stats.note: Kazakhstan was the second-largest source of natural uranium for EU utilities in 2025, supplying about a fifth of all deliveries.
stats.detail: EU utilities purchased 2,981 tonnes of uranium (tU) originating in Kazakhstan in 2025, equal to 20.31 percent of the 14,678 tU total delivered to EU utilities that year. This was a decline of 12.11 percent in quantity from 2024, even as total EU deliveries rose slightly, reflecting a shift in supplier shares rather than a shrinking overall market. Kazakhstan, along with Canada, Russia and Uzbekistan, is one of the top suppliers whose deliveries the Euratom Supply Agency tracks by country of origin and chemical/physical form as part of its annual market survey of EU nuclear utilities.

questions.text: When a low-carbon grid hits its hardest week of the year, what has to be running for the lights to stay on?
questions.why: Both camps agree wind and solar are the cheapest energy to add. They divide over whether storage and transmission can bridge multi-day lulls, or whether that gap requires generation that runs regardless of weather.
questions.detail: Nuclear supplied 2,602 terawatt-hours in 2023, about 9 percent of global electricity and the second largest low-carbon source after hydroelectricity. The dispute is not about the cheap first half of a clean grid: the IEA and NEA estimate the levelized cost of electricity from a new nuclear plant at 69 USD/MWh, against a median of 50 for onshore wind and 56 for utility-scale solar, so on a per-unit basis the variable sources win the early build-out and few people contest it. It is about the windless, overcast stretches that last days across a whole region. One reading treats those as a problem of scale and geography, answered by long transmission, storage, demand that shifts in time and deliberate overbuilding whose surplus is spilled, each with a falling cost curve. The other treats deep lulls as a feature of weather that hours of batteries cannot bridge, and concludes that a system without weather-independent output keeps gas plants on standby and burns them, making the real comparison nuclear against gas rather than nuclear against wind and solar. Hourly modeling over many real weather years, and the behavior of grids that have pushed variable renewables well past half their supply, are what could decide it.

questions.text: What decides whether the second, fifth and tenth reactor of a design costs less to build than the first?
questions.why: One reading blames Western overruns on one-off designs, stop-start programs and regulatory churn, all fixable by repetition. The other holds that complexity and safety margins push costs up as fast as repetition pushes them down.
questions.detail: Western projects supply the case for structural cost. Vogtle Units 3 and 4 rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion, and the main contractor, Westinghouse, filed for bankruptcy mid-construction. Hinkley Point C is now projected at 35 billion pounds in 2015 prices, roughly 48 billion in 2026 prices, almost double the estimate when the project was approved, with Unit 1 delayed to 2030. Against this, an independent analysis puts the average capital cost of China’s operating reactors at about 2,230 US dollars per kilowatt, the Hualong One now has 41 units approved, under construction or in operation worldwide, and the four Barakah units were contracted for about 20.4 billion dollars, largely under a fixed-price arrangement. One reading takes the second group as proof that a stable order book, a single design and a retained workforce remove the overruns. The other argues the comparison hides differences in labor costs, financing, liability and regulatory independence, so the lesson may not travel. What would settle it is whether unit costs fall along an identifiable curve inside one program, rather than across selected cases.

questions.text: How should a small chance of a rare, irreversible disaster be weighed against harm that arrives steadily and unremarked?
questions.why: One reading says deaths and emissions per terawatt-hour are the only honest common scale. The other says displacement, land loss and dread are a different kind of harm that disappears when it is averaged into a rate.
questions.detail: The per-unit case is straightforward. Nuclear’s historical death rate is 0.03 per terawatt-hour, second only to solar among energy sources, and its median life-cycle emission intensity is 12 grams of CO2 equivalent per kilowatt-hour, against 820 for coal and 490 for gas. Those rates rest on choices: the comparison assumes a death toll of 433 from Chernobyl and 2,314 from Fukushima, the latter almost entirely evacuation-related. UNSCEAR found that Fukushima released only about 10 percent of Chernobyl’s radioiodine and radiocaesium, and that thyroid doses to evacuees were about 100 times lower. One reading says a rate per terawatt-hour is the only way to compare sources without privileging the accidents that make news over the coal smoke that does not. The other says an accident that empties a district for a generation is not the same kind of harm as a statistical shortening of many lives, that the evacuation deaths themselves show how much of the damage runs through fear and disruption, and that no arithmetic tells a society how much insurance to buy against the tail of a distribution.

questions.text: What would have to happen before a country could say its high-level waste problem is finished rather than deferred?
questions.why: One reading holds deep geological disposal is technically demonstrated and only politics remains. The other holds that nothing has yet been loaded, sealed and observed, so the demonstration is still a design.
questions.detail: There are no commercial-scale purpose-built underground high-level waste repositories in operation anywhere in the world, and almost 400,000 tons of spent fuel have been produced since the 1950s, with two-thirds remaining in temporary storage. Finland is closest. At Onkalo, used fuel will be placed in bedrock about 430 meters down, in a tightly sealed iron-copper canister surrounded by a bentonite buffer, with tunnels backfilled by swellable clay. The construction cost has so far been around 1 billion euros, with an estimated 4 billion more to operate the site for one hundred years and eventually close it. One reading says the physics and engineering are settled, the corrosion and transport behavior have been modeled for decades, and what remains is the political work of finding willing hosts. The other says a design is not a result, that no repository has been filled and sealed, that the relevant timescales exceed any institution that has ever existed, and that interim storage at reactor sites is the de facto policy almost everywhere. Both readings have to say what evidence could ever confirm a hundred-thousand-year claim.

questions.text: When a reactor ends up costing far more than promised, who should be left holding the overrun?
questions.why: One reading treats firm clean capacity as infrastructure that only public risk-bearing can finance. The other says a project that cannot clear a competitive market should not be charged to captive ratepayers and taxpayers.
questions.detail: A reactor is a capital project whose price is dominated by interest accumulating over a long build, so who carries the risk sets the cost. The US government has given 8.3 billion dollars of loan guarantees to help finance construction of the Vogtle reactors. In Britain, the National Audit Office estimated that projected consumer top-up payments for Hinkley Point C rose from 6.1 billion pounds in October 2013, when the strike price was agreed, to 29.7 billion in 2016, and to 50 billion in July 2017 as forecast energy prices fell. One reading treats guarantees, contracts for difference and rate-base recovery as the ordinary tools states use for long-lived assets no merchant market will fund, and points out that without them nothing gets built at all. The other says these instruments move overrun risk onto people who cannot exit, reward optimistic estimates and remove the discipline that would stop a failing project, and notes that long-term operation of existing plants is the least-cost dispatchable option at 32 USD/MWh while new build is estimated at 69. At bottom the question is who should be exposed when the estimate is wrong.

questions.text: Whose agreement has to be obtained before a mine, a plant or a repository is placed on a particular piece of land?
questions.why: One reading holds that national climate and security need cannot leave every locality a veto, since delay is itself a harm. The other holds that host communities and Indigenous nations retain a real veto over what is put on their land.
questions.detail: The fuel cycle touches land at three points, mining, generation and disposal, and each concentrates the burden on particular people while the benefit is national. In South Australia, 27 Native Title groups from around the state held a vote, and it was unanimous that they did not want a nuclear waste dump. Consent can also run the other way: an independent poll found Pennsylvanians favor restarting the Three Mile Island plant by a more than two to one margin, and that 70 percent of state residents support the continued use of nuclear energy. One reading argues that a climate and security emergency cannot grant a veto to every locality, that permitting delay is paid in emissions elsewhere, and that compensation plus a fair national process is the legitimate settlement. The other argues that downwinders, host towns and Indigenous nations have historically absorbed the costs of the fuel cycle without ever agreeing to them, and that consent is not a procedural box but the condition on which a facility can be tolerated for a century. Behind both sits the question of what consent means when the facility outlasts everyone who gave it.

questions.text: What changes, in cost and in waste, when a reactor is made small enough to be built in a factory?
questions.why: One reading expects serial factory production to undercut large plants once volume arrives. The other expects a smaller reactor to carry the same safety systems and staffing over less output, and to leave more waste per unit.
questions.detail: Small modular reactors trade the economies of size for the economies of number, which exist only if the number arrives. An SMR factory would require substantial upfront capital, and per-unit costs would only become economical when an estimated 40 to 70 units are produced. NuScale had an agreement to build reactors in Idaho by 2030, but it was cancelled in 2023 after the estimated cost rose from 3.6 billion to 9.3 billion dollars, before any factory existed. Waste divides the same way. Krall, Macfarlane and Ewing found that small modular reactors will generate at least nine times more neutron-activated steel than conventional power plants, and analyses report some designs producing more than five times the spent fuel per kilowatt and up to thirty-five times more neutron-activation waste. NuScale replied that the paper used outdated design information for the energy capacity of its fuel and wrong assumptions about the reflector material and fuel burnup, and the IAEA holds that countries with established programs and existing infrastructure should be able to manage SMR spent fuel. One side sees a chicken-and-egg problem an order book solves; the other sees physics working against smallness.

questions.text: How long does it take to build a fuel and vendor supply chain that does not run through Russia or China?
questions.why: One reading sees substitution as a matter of money and a few years, already underway. The other sees four separate bottlenecks with long lead times, where diversification often means another concentrated supplier.
questions.detail: Rosatom accounted for 23 of 31 orders for new reactors placed between 2009 and 2018, and serves as a one-stop shop across the fuel cycle, from reactor materials to uranium enrichment and waste disposal. In 2023, 38 percent of enriched uranium for EU nuclear power plants was imported from Russia. The Euratom Supply Agency reports that the EU’s nuclear fuel supply chain is heavily dependent on imports of uranium, while enrichment, conversion and fuel fabrication are more diversified inside the EU, with Kazakhstan supplying 20.31 percent of EU natural uranium deliveries in 2025. It also reports that by the end of 2025 all EU operators of VVER reactors had secured alternative fuel supply contracts from non-Russian suppliers. One reading takes that as evidence substitution works once it is paid for, so the constraint is money and years rather than physics. The other notes that mining, conversion, enrichment and fabrication are four distinct bottlenecks with few suppliers and long lead times, that replacing one concentrated source often means creating another, and that a reactor ordered today fixes a fuel relationship for sixty years.

questions.text: Is there a general verdict to be had about nuclear power at all, or only verdicts about particular projects?
questions.why: One reading says policy needs a class-level judgment, since taxonomies and procurement cannot wait for each project. The other says the class contains objects too unlike each other for a general verdict to predict anything.
questions.detail: The evidence itself raises the question. The same broad technology delivered four units at Barakah for about 20.4 billion dollars, a plant now generating about 40 TWh a year, roughly 25 percent of UAE electricity, while two units at Vogtle rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion. Life extension of an existing plant is the least-cost dispatchable option at 32 USD/MWh, while a new plant is estimated at 69. One reading says a class-level verdict is exactly what policy instruments need, because taxonomies, portfolio standards and capital allocation cannot be re-argued project by project, and a fifty-year Western record of overruns has told you what you need to know. The other says a first-of-a-kind in a liberalized market, the tenth unit of a series under a state utility and the restart of a plant already built are different objects, so a general verdict mostly reimports the conclusion you began with. California’s regulator leans the second way: staff propose a clean energy standard whose requirements do not unfairly discriminate across technology types or projects, and state law directs the commission to procure by attribute on a nondiscriminatory basis.

positions.name: Build new reactors as climate infrastructure
positions.steelman: There is no credible path to climate stabilization without a substantial role for nuclear power: build firm, zero-carbon reactors programmatically, fleet by fleet, alongside wind and solar, or gas fills the gap they leave.
positions.description: Nuclear supplied 2,602 terawatt hours in 2023, about 9 percent of global electricity, at a median life-cycle intensity of 12 grams of CO2 equivalent per kilowatt-hour, against 820 for coal and 490 for gas. This camp holds that such firm, zero-carbon output must grow rather than shrink. Wind and solar lead; nuclear complements them, in the International Energy Agency’s words, as low emissions electricity available on demand. Where reliable plants close, most economies revert to fossil fuel, not to storage. The instrument is programmatic newbuild: a committed fleet of identical units with stable finance, so each build is faster and cheaper than the last, instead of one-off projects separated by decades that lose the workforce and the supply chain in between. The UK’s stated ambition of up to 24 GW by 2050 is the shape of the ask.
positions.detail: The reasoning starts from what a grid must do. Nuclear’s historical death rate is 0.03 deaths per terawatt-hour, second only to solar, so the live objections are cost and delivery, not safety or carbon. Those the camp treats as symptoms of stop-start ordering. EDF reports that repeating identical work on Hinkley Point C’s second unit improves performance by 20 to 30 percent; an independent analysis puts China’s operating fleet at about 2,230 US dollars per kilowatt; the UAE’s four Barakah units were contracted for about 20.4 billion dollars, largely at fixed price, and now supply about 25 percent of the country’s electricity. Fleets work; one-offs do not. On the alternatives, the IEA’s Fatih Birol has said that without nuclear there is no chance of reaching climate targets on time. The camp concedes the record it is judged by. Vogtle rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion and its main contractor went bankrupt mid-construction; Hinkley Point C is projected at 35 billion pounds in 2015 prices, almost double the approval estimate; NuScale’s Idaho project was cancelled in 2023 after its estimate rose from 3.6 to 9.3 billion dollars. It concedes too that no commercial-scale purpose-built high-level waste repository is yet in operation anywhere. None of this changes the conclusion, because these are first-of-a-kind builds in countries that stopped building for a generation, and Finland’s Onkalo, placing used fuel about 430 meters down in sealed iron-copper canisters, shows that disposal is an engineering problem now being solved.
positions.proponents: Nuclear Energy Institute, International Energy Agency, Fatih Birol, James Hansen, Ken Caldeira, Kerry Emanuel, Tom Wigley, George Monbiot, Tom Greatrex (UK Nuclear Industry Association), China National Nuclear Corporation (Hualong One), North America’s Building Trades Unions, W. Gyude Moore

positions.name: Replace nuclear with renewables, storage and efficiency
positions.steelman: Every dollar and every year has one best use: wind, solar, storage, transmission and efficiency cut more carbon faster than any reactor can, so build those, stop new nuclear, and retire the existing fleet alongside the coal and gas plants.
positions.description: The case rests on opportunity cost. Protecting the climate means abating the most carbon at the least cost and in the least time, and on that test renewables win by a wide margin. Amory Lovins writes that “in over 24,000 actual market projects, new unsubsidized renewables make electricity 5–13 times cheaper than nuclear newbuild according to BNEF; merchant bank Lazard analysis finds 3–8 times.” Mark Jacobson puts it in output terms: “Every dollar spent on nuclear results in one-fifth the energy one would gain with wind or solar [at the same cost], and nuclear energy takes five to 17 years longer before it becomes available.” Money and skilled labor committed to a reactor are not available for turbines, panels, batteries, transmission and efficiency, which deliver sooner. So capital should go where it abates fastest, and the existing fleet should retire alongside coal and gas.
positions.detail:
The speed argument does the same work as the cost argument. Greenpeace estimates that doubling world nuclear capacity by 2050 would cut greenhouse gas emissions by only about 4 percent, and would require bringing 37 large reactors to the grid every year, against the few to 10 grid connections a year the last decade actually delivered; average construction time since 2009 has been just under 10 years. Meanwhile, on the World Nuclear Industry Status Report’s figures, levelized costs over the past decade fell 88 percent for utility-scale solar and 69 percent for wind and rose 23 percent for nuclear. Small reactors do not rescue the schedule; IEEFA finds they “still look to be too expensive, too slow to build, and too risky to play a significant role in transitioning from fossil fuels in the coming 10-15 years.”
On reliability, the camp answers that grids are balanced by efficiency, flexible demand, storage and interconnection rather than by baseload plants, and that Germany’s exit bore this out: Robert Habeck said “We see today that our power supply is secure, that power price dropped also after the nuclear phase-out and that CO2 emissions are going down as well.” It concedes that reactors emit little carbon in operation and that a paid-off reactor looks cheap per megawatt-hour. That does not change the conclusion: the subsidies keeping such plants open are contested — FirstEnergy paid $61 million in bribes to win a $1 billion Ohio bailout — and no commercial-scale high-level waste repository is in operation anywhere in the world.
positions.proponents: Greenpeace International, the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis, Amory Lovins, M.V. Ramana, Mark Jacobson, the European Environmental Bureau, Robert Habeck, Georgia WAND, David Schwartzman

positions.name: Run the existing reactors longer, build no new ones
positions.steelman: The cheapest, fastest firm low-carbon power on any grid is the reactor already standing: relicense it, restart it, contract it. New construction can wait until someone shows it can be built on schedule without the public carrying the risk.
positions.description: Electricity from the long-term operation of existing nuclear plants was found to be the least-cost dispatchable option at 32 USD/MWh, against 69 USD/MWh for a new plant. The first move in a serious decarbonization plan is therefore to keep what already runs: extend licenses, restart recently closed units while the equipment, the license and the workforce still exist, and sign long-term contracts for firm carbon-free output. Nuclear power is the single largest source of low-carbon electricity in the United States, and the Union of Concerned Scientists found that nearly 35 percent of the country’s nuclear plants are at risk of early closure or slated to retire, and that closing them could raise US power-sector emissions by 4 to 6 percent. A reactor lost to gas is a measurable step backward; a reactor not yet built is a promise with a long record of overruns behind it.
positions.detail:
The argument is comparative. The hazards of the operating fleet are known and regulated — UCS found that today’s nuclear reactors achieved the NRC’s top safety rating 80 percent of the time — while new designs are still experimental. Edwin Lyman argues that small modular reactors will generate more expensive electricity than large reactors, which themselves are not economical to build at present: Vogtle 3 and 4 rose from a certified $14 billion to about $34 billion, and NuScale’s Idaho project was cancelled in 2023 after its estimate rose from $3.6 billion to $9.3 billion. Retiring a working reactor is a subtraction: Thierry Breton described shutting down operational nuclear power plants as depriving Europe of low-carbon energy capacity, and Veronika Grimm said power prices “of course” would be lower if nuclear plants were kept running.

Instruments differ. UCS wants carbon pricing or a low-carbon electricity standard, with support conditioned on consumer protection and safety; the restart wing prefers private money, as in the 20-year agreement with Microsoft that Constellation announced in September 2024, which the company says will add about 835 megawatts of carbon-free energy to the grid at the Crane Clean Energy Center. The camp concedes that some plants are unprofitable — UCS put the cost of bringing them to breakeven at $814 million a year — and splits on whether paying it is acceptable. It concedes too that Germany’s exit brought no immediate crisis, and that the lost reactors’ 2024 price effect was estimated at 0.3 ct/kWh. Neither changes the conclusion, because the cheapest firm low-carbon power is already standing.
positions.proponents: Union of Concerned Scientists, Edwin Lyman, Joseph Lassiter (Harvard, retired), Joe Dominguez (Constellation), Bobby Hollis (Microsoft), Rob Bair (Pennsylvania State Building and Construction Trades Council), Thierry Breton, Veronika Grimm

positions.name: Mass-produce small modular reactors
positions.steelman: Nuclear got expensive because every plant is a one-off megaproject. Shrink the reactor, build the same unit in a factory over and over, and construction time, site-specific overruns and financing risk fall together, as they do in every other manufactured product.
positions.description: Nuclear power is expensive not because of physics but because of how plants are built: as bespoke megaprojects, each effectively a first of a kind, financed over a decade before earning a cent. Vogtle Units 3 and 4 rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion, and Hinkley Point C is now projected at 35 billion pounds in 2015 prices, almost double the estimate at approval. Shrink the unit below 300 megawatts, fabricate it in a factory, ship it and repeat, and the learning curve that governs aircraft and turbines begins to apply to reactors. Modules can be added as demand grows, so no utility has to stake its balance sheet on a single ten-year build. Alvin Weinberg put the argument in 1952: with many small units, industry “would edge into the business a little at a time and at each stage would be able to match its risk with its financial capability.”
positions.detail:
The mechanism is serial production. A factory that builds the same module again and again turns construction into manufacturing: site work shrinks, custom components disappear, welders repeat work they have already done, and units can be built in parallel rather than end to end. Bret Kugelmass argues that thousands of SMRs could be built in parallel, “thus reducing costs associated with long borrowing times for prolonged construction schedules and reducing risk premiums currently linked to large projects”. A second wing points to a market gigawatt plants cannot serve: David Mohre of the NRECA Energy and Power Division said SMRs like NuScale’s are ideal for rural towns that need small power plants, and the same logic now draws data centers. Smaller cores also carry less decay heat to remove after shutdown, and regulators have accepted the case. NuScale remains the only SMR technology company to have received design approval from the NRC, and in May 2025 it won a second approval, for its uprated 77 MWe module.

The camp concedes the record so far. NuScale’s Idaho project was cancelled in 2023 after its estimate rose from 3.6 billion to 9.3 billion dollars, and factory economics only reach per-unit affordability at an estimated 40 to 70 units. That is a first-of-a-kind problem, not a refutation of the curve. The Nuclear Energy Institute put it plainly after the cancellation: “Innovation — particularly in new technologies — is defined by fits and starts. And innovation in next-generation nuclear is no different.” On waste, NuScale says the critical study used outdated design information for the energy capacity of its fuel and wrong assumptions on reflector material and burnup, and the IAEA’s Christophe Xerri says SMR spent fuel can be managed in the same way as that of large reactors.
positions.proponents: NuScale Power, Craig Piercy (American Nuclear Society), the Nuclear Energy Institute, Bret Kugelmass (Energy Impact Center), Jon Ball (GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy), Simon Irish (Terrestrial Energy), Christophe Xerri (IAEA), David Mohre (NRECA)

positions.name: Judge each project on its measured attributes
positions.steelman: Cost, firmness and safety are attributes of a particular plant, in a particular market, under a particular regulator, not of a fuel. Judge the project in front of you on what it measurably delivers, and buy the attributes you need without naming a technology.
positions.description: The unit of decision is a project, not a technology. What a plant costs, how firmly it delivers and how safe it is are properties of a specific design at a specific site, with a specific supply chain and a specific regulator, and those properties vary more within nuclear than between nuclear and its rivals. The U.S. Energy Information Administration states that “Direct comparisons of LCOE or LCOS across technologies are misleading as a method to assess the economic competitiveness.” Hinkley Point C’s technical director said in 2019 that “In effect HPC is a first-of-a-kind plant in a country that has not built a new plant for three decades.” The practical program follows from that: technology-inclusive licensing, procurement written in attributes rather than fuel names, and findings made case by case on measured performance rather than on a verdict about the fuel.
positions.detail:
The camp’s evidence is the spread inside the category. The IEA and NEA put new nuclear at 69 USD/MWh and long-term operation of an existing reactor at 32; EIA projects advanced nuclear entering service in 2031 at 87.81 USD/MWh, against 56.75 for onshore wind. Vogtle 3 and 4 rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion, while Barakah’s four units were contracted for about 20.4 billion, largely fixed-price, and an independent analysis puts China’s operating fleet at about 2,230 USD per kilowatt. Hinkley’s second unit is being built 20 to 30 percent faster than the first. Figures that far apart are not measurements of one thing. A verdict on the fuel cannot be read off them; a verdict on a named design, sponsor, site and schedule can.

The alternatives skip that step, generalizing from cross-technology averages to a judgment about a class. EIA’s own remedy is to pair cost with value: “LCOE is limited because it only reflects the cost to build and operate a plant, not the value of the plant to the grid.” The NRC’s part 53 is a technology-inclusive framework “that can be used for any reactor technology, any size reactor, and any reactor end use.” BASE, reviewing 136 reactor and SMR concepts, concludes that “it is not possible to state, that a higher safety level is achieved by SMR concepts in principle.” CPUC staff, proposing a new procurement program for California, write that its options are designed to satisfy a fairness principle under which “Program requirements are fairly distributed across LSEs and do not unfairly discriminate across technology types or projects.” The camp concedes that the class-level facts are real: a median life-cycle intensity of 12 g CO2eq/kWh, a historical death rate of 0.03 per TWh. They simply do not tell a regulator whether to license this design, or a buyer whether to sign this contract.
positions.proponents: U.S. Energy Information Administration, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, California Public Utilities Commission staff, German Federal Office for the Safety of Nuclear Waste Management (BASE), the technical director of Hinkley Point C

positions.name: Require the consent of host and mining nations
positions.steelman: No mine, mill, reactor or dump on our country without our consent, and consent means the right to refuse — whatever the national energy accounting says.
positions.description: Consent means the power to say no. No exploration, mine, mill, ore route, reactor or repository belongs on a people’s country unless the people whose country it is have agreed, and a process that gathers views and then proceeds anyway is not agreement. The Navajo Nation enacted a statute in 2008 placing a moratorium on uranium mining on its lands, and Stephen Etsitty of the Navajo Nation Environmental Protection Agency says of it that “it can’t happen here, not within our jurisdiction.” In South Australia, Tauto Sansbury, chairperson of the Aboriginal Congress of South Australia, described a meeting with the state’s Royal Commissioner at which “we had 27 Native Title groups from all around South Australia. We had a vote on it. And it was unanimous that the vote said no we don’t want it.” Navajo Nation President Buu Nygren has put it plainly: “I don’t think anybody on the Navajo would be willing to entertain nuclear energy”. These are not objections to a design detail. They are refusals of the activity, grounded in what the fuel chain has already done to the people living nearest to it.
positions.detail:
The case rests on a mismatch between who bears the fuel chain and who counts its benefits. Mining, milling, ore transport and disposal fall on particular places, many of them Indigenous, while the electricity and the avoided emissions are added up nationally. The European Commission’s SCHEER, reviewing nuclear power for the EU taxonomy, held that “dependence on an operational regulatory framework is not in itself sufficient to mitigate these impacts, e.g. in mining and milling where the burden of the impacts are felt outside Europe.” A regulator that cannot certify harms falling outside its borders plainly cannot consent on behalf of those who carry them. The memory is specific, not abstract. Karina Lester, of the Yankunytjatjara Native Title Aboriginal Corporation, wrote that many members “are descendants of or directly been impacted by the use of Nuclear Energy, in particular Maralinga in the 1950’s and 60’s, and we firmly say NO NUCLEAR ENERGY FOR SOUTH AUSTRALIA.”

Grant the low-carbon case and the safety statistics: they do not answer whose country is dug up and whose descendants keep watch over the waste. Kokatha Aboriginal Corporation told the royal commission that it is “strongly opposed to any level of storage of medium and high level radioactive waste on their traditional country”, and Rebecca Bear-Wingfield observed that there “isn’t a high level waste dump in operation anywhere in the world”. That last point still holds: no commercial-scale purpose-built high-level repository is in operation anywhere. Against those who count permitting delay as itself a harm, the reply is that a refusal is not a delay to be engineered around; it is the answer.
positions.proponents: Navajo Nation (Stephen Etsitty, President Buu Nygren), Kokatha Aboriginal Corporation, Karina Lester of the Yankunytjatjara Native Title Aboriginal Corporation, Sue Coleman-Haseldine, Rebecca Bear-Wingfield, and the European Commission’s SCHEER

crux.lead: Is the cost of a reactor a fact about the technology or about the way it has been bought — and who carries the risk while that stays unsettled?
crux.lead_highlight: about the technology or about the way it has been bought
crux.subtitle: Almost nobody in this debate disputes the headline numbers: nuclear’s median life-cycle intensity is 12 grams of CO2 equivalent per kilowatt-hour against 820 for coal, wind and solar are cheaper per unit of energy added, and recent Western builds have overrun badly — Vogtle Units 3 and 4 rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion. The split is over what that record predicts, and over who should hold the bill and the site while the answer comes in.
crux.empirical: Both camps read the same construction record. Vogtle Units 3 and 4 rose from a certified 14 billion dollars to about 34 billion, with the main contractor, Westinghouse, going bankrupt mid-construction; Hinkley Point C is now projected at 35 billion pounds in 2015 prices, almost double the estimate at approval; NuScale’s Idaho project was canceled in 2023 after its estimate rose from 3.6 billion to 9.3 billion dollars. The fork is what that record is evidence of. One reading takes it as the signature of a stop-start industry that builds every plant as a first of a kind and disperses its workforce in between, so that repetition is the cure; it points to the Hualong One, with 41 units approved, under construction or in operation worldwide, to an independent analysis putting the average capital cost of China’s operating reactors at about 2,230 USD per kilowatt, and to Barakah, whose four units were contracted for about 20.4 billion dollars, largely under a fixed-price arrangement, and which now provide about 25 percent of UAE electricity. The other reading takes complexity and safety margin to push cost up roughly as fast as repetition pushes it down, and reads those foreign numbers as traveling with their labor markets, finance and state risk-bearing rather than with the design. The rest of the argument inherits the fork. Whether a factory beats a construction site depends on volume: per-unit costs are estimated to become economical only at 40 to 70 units. Whether waste is finished or deferred depends on demonstration, and no commercial-scale purpose-built high-level waste repository is in operation anywhere in the world. And how much firm output a grid needs in its hardest week, which sets what any of this is worth, is not settled by anything either side can yet point to.
crux.values: The second branch is about how harm is counted, and who gets to count it. On the common scale nuclear has a death rate of 0.03 per TWh, second only to solar among energy sources, a figure built by assuming a death toll of 433 from Chernobyl and 2,314 from Fukushima. What is in dispute is not the arithmetic but the averaging. A rate per terawatt-hour spreads harm smoothly over a population; what the fuel chain actually does is concentrate a small chance of an irreversible event, together with a mine, a mill, an ore route and a repository, on particular places and particular people, mostly rural, often Indigenous. To one side, declining to convert those into a rate is a failure of seriousness: the fossil alternative kills steadily and unremarked, delay is itself a harm, and a national grid cannot leave every locality a veto. To the other, the conversion is where the moral content leaks out: displacement, land loss and dread are different in kind from a rate, consent means the power to refuse, and a people whose country has already been mined owes nothing to the national accounting. Twenty-seven Native Title groups across South Australia voted unanimously against a nuclear waste dump. The same structure governs money. The US government provided 8.3 billion dollars in loan guarantees to finance the Vogtle reactors, and the UK National Audit Office found projected consumer top-up payments for Hinkley Point C rose from 6.1 billion pounds in 2013 to 50 billion in 2017. Either firm clean capacity is infrastructure whose risk the public properly carries because no private balance sheet will, or a project that cannot clear a competitive market is a bill sent to people who never chose it — and nothing in the cost data decides which.
